doc.title: Bobby Shew interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 1, 2020

title: Teaching players to play scales with emotion
summary: Shew describes his sorrow, anger and happy scale exercise and criticises practicing only for technical facility.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Yeah. Hell no, their life is on the line at all times. You know I’ve known, I won’t mention any names here because I love them, but I know some very prominent orchestral people, not only trumpet players but others too, that live and die by that sword. They sit there and they’re in constant sweating. And especially if it’s a long period where they can’t play for — they’ve got tacet sheets and they’ve got to wait out for 400 measures during the violin solo or something, and then you’ve got to suddenly come in and it’s marcato and it’s [scats] and you’ve got to come in and hit a high D or something, and you sit there and you start worrying about that. The future is like looming at you and it’s like dragons on your shoulders and stuff, you know. And then you look and there’s Ozawa up there glaring at everybody, and oh for Christ’s sake you know. But I swear to you, but the whole point about it is that when I teach, when I teach [gestures quotes] I use quotes around that word because I don’t really, I just try to inspire more than anything. But the

whole idea is I try to make sure that people understand the value of playing everything with some emotion in it. That little example, I think the story that you are referring to is it’s just a little maked up game I play when I do a lecture on improvisation is the thing. But it’s not only about improvisation, it’s just picking up the horn and playing period. But it is that you know you can pretend, I take three emotions: sorrow, angry and happy. And I have them play the scale like sorrowfully. And I say pretend that the neighbor ran over your cat you know and oh my God I love that cat. Get that emotion going, and I love that cat. Now play that scale thinking about your favorite cat and try to make sure that the way you approach that scale, it’s not like [scats] that’s not sorrowful. Emotion has to do with a vibration in the body and everything. And you get down into sorrow and apathy and things like that, it goes very slow. Whereas if you’re angry, if you say that neighbor I’m going to kill him, he drives like an idiot, I’m gonna — he ran over my cat I’m going to kill him. Now play that scale [scats]. Baseball bat to the head. Okay? And then you say wait a minute, that’s not my cat, and now you play happy [scats]. And so just as it’s a silly example but it gets the point across very easily not only to children but to adults as well who sit there and say God what have I been doing all these years?

You know you open up the Arban book and you play scales and stuff, all you’re doing is trying to accumulate huge amounts of technical facility in hopes, and when your attention is on you in the practice room, what is your goal? Damn I hope I don’t miss any notes here today. You know?
